newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Jamaica reaches drug accord with U.S..
newsitem.headline: Jamaica reaches drug accord with U.S..

text.p: Prime Minister P.J. Patterson announced on Monday that Jamaica and the United States had agreed on a final text for a drug interdiction accord, a greatly truncated version of the original that Washington had signed with most other countries in the region.
Jamaica last year refused to sign the so-called "shiprider" agreement, which would have allowed U.S. drug enforcement agents to operate in Jamaica's territorial waters and air space.

The decision led to threats from Washington to "decertify" Jamaica's drug interdiction efforts and sparked an emergency summit in December of the 14-member Caribbean Community, of which Jamaica is a member.
"Certification" is an annual evaluation by Washington in which the United States judges the antinarcotics efforts of other nations.
President Bill Clinton will meet Caribbean leaders during his current trip to Mexico, Costa Rica and Barbados.
"The agreement makes clear there can be no random patrolling of the maritime waters or air space of Jamaica," Patterson told reporters.
U.S. authorities will be required to apply on a "case-by-case" basis before being allowed, or denied, permission to board and search vessels.
Such operations, when approved, will be under the command and direction of Jamaican law enforcement officials and be carried out according to Jamaican law, he said.

On those occasions where U.S. agents are in "hot pursuit" of suspected traffickers and cannot apply for permission, Patterson said they will be allowed into Jamaican waters or air space but only to maintain contact.
"There can be no interdiction," the prime minister stated.
Jamaica, Barbados, Surinam and Haiti have so far refused to sign the "shiprider" accords, saying they violate national sovereignty. Patterson was also critical of the U.S. certification process.

"We have to move away from making unilateral evaluations and then seeking to impose them on other sovereign states," he said, suggesting collective decisions should be taken "as equals on vital issues."
